edges.description: The ingested amino acid is metabolised to the species that does the damage. Hypoglycin A is a protoxin; nothing happens until the body converts it.
MCPA-CoA is itself the inhibitor. Unlike a normal substrate it is not turned over into a product; it reacts with the enzyme and stays.
With the dehydrogenases inactivated, the beta-oxidation spiral cannot turn.
Without beta-oxidation the liver has neither the acetyl-CoA to make ketones nor the reducing equivalents and ATP that gluconeogenesis runs on.
With neither route available, blood glucose falls and is not defended.

nodes.description: Covalent, irreversible inactivation of acyl-CoA dehydrogenases. MCPA-CoA modifies the enzyme's FAD, taking activity to under 2 percent, and the modification is not reversed by removing the compound. This is the node the whole entry turns on, and it is where the poisoning and the inherited disease become the same problem.

evidence.reference_title: Inactivation of general acyl-CoA dehydrogenase from pig kidney by a metabolite of hypoglycin A.
evidence.snippet: Pig kidney general acyl-CoA dehydrogenase is irreversibly inactivated by methylenecyclopropylacetyl-CoA, a metabolite of the hypoglycemic amino acid hypoglycin from Blighia sapida, to less that 2% of native activity.

evidence.reference_title: Inactivation of general acyl-CoA dehydrogenase from pig kidney by a metabolite of hypoglycin A.
evidence.snippet: During inactivation, about 80% of the enzyme FAD is covalently and irreversibly modified with the residual inhibition possibly resulting from modification of the protein.

evidence.reference_title: Selective inhibition of acyl-CoA dehydrogenases by a metabolite of hypoglycin.
evidence.snippet: Extracts of liver mitochondria from donor rats given hypoglycin, the toxic amino acid from the ackee plant (Blighia sapida) showed drastically reduced levels of acyl-CoA dehydrogenase activity with butyryl-CoA as substrate.

nodes.description: A naturally occurring poisoning, not an engineered model. Horses grazing pastures with Acer seeds eat hypoglycin A, activate it to the same MCPA-CoA, and develop the same acquired multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency. It is the source of most of the quantitative biochemistry available for this toxin, because horses present in numbers and are sampled, and human ackee poisoning is sporadic and rarely sampled at the bench.

nodes.description: The two fasting responses fail together. Ketone bodies are not made, so the brain has no alternative fuel, and glucose is not made, so the supply is not replaced. This is why the hypoglycaemia is described as profound rather than merely present, and why it recurs after correction while the enzyme block lasts.
Profound, and hypoketotic - the absence of ketones alongside the low glucose is the finding that points at a fatty acid oxidation block rather than at any ordinary cause.

nodes.description: The beta-oxidation spiral stalls across multiple chain lengths. Acyl groups back up and leave as dicarboxylic acids and acylcarnitines, which is what makes the poisoning legible in a urine or blood sample - and legible as an inherited disease, because the profile is the one those diseases produce.

nodes.description: Eating the fruit of Blighia sapida before it has opened naturally. Ripening is the detoxification step: hypoglycin A falls as the fruit matures and the pods open on their own, so the traditional rule about never forcing a pod is a food-safety practice with a biochemical basis. Exposure also occurs through canned product, which is how the disease reaches countries where the tree does not grow.

nodes.description: Conversion of hypoglycin A to methylenecyclopropylacetyl-CoA. This is a bioactivation poisoning: the parent amino acid is not the inhibitor, and the CoA thioester is. Its free acid, MCPA, is what appears in the urine of poisoned patients and its carnitine conjugate is what is measured in serum.
